title: Numbers & shopping
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: The price question agrees with the THING, never with the person asking: ¿Cuánto cuesta el café? · ¿Cuánto cuestan los libros? This is M1's gustar all over again — what is bought is the subject of the verb, and the buyer is nowhere in the sentence. One thing takes cuesta, more than one takes cuestan.
cuánto in front of cuesta or cuestan is "how much" and stays exactly as it is. Put it in front of a noun and it agrees with that noun like any adjective: ¿Cuántos libros? · ¿Cuántas manzanas?

One number has three shapes. uno stands alone when nothing follows it — Quiero uno — and shortens in front of a noun: un libro (m) · una mesa (f). *uno libro is the mistake, and it is the only number that does this.

A quantity is tied to what it is a quantity OF by de, with no article in between: un kilo de manzanas, una botella de agua. English says "a kilo of apples" the same way and then drops the "of" in "a water bottle" — Spanish never drops it.

por favor is a fixed two-word politeness that travels whole, and it sits at the edge of the request, usually at the end after a comma: Quiero dos cafés, por favor. Neither half means anything useful on its own here.

muy and mucho are not interchangeable. muy goes in front of an adjective and never changes shape — muy caro, muy cara, muy caros. mucho goes with a noun or after a verb and does change — mucho pan, muchas manzanas, trabajo mucho. English "very" and "a lot" sort them out; *muy mucho and *trabajo muy are what happens when they are swapped.

A price adjective agrees with the noun it describes, exactly as M3's colours did: el libro es caro · la manzana es cara · los libros son caros. The ending belongs to the thing being priced, not to whoever is complaining about it.

Both es caro and está caro are real Spanish, and they say different things. El libro es caro classifies the book as an expensive thing; El libro está caro says it is pricey just now, this week, at this stall. This module says es, because it is talking about what things cost in general — not because estar is forbidden.

Numbers themselves do not change for gender or number: dos cafés, ocho manzanas, diez libros. Counting upwards is vocabulary rather than grammar — dos, tres, cuatro, cinco … diez, veinte, cien — and the only shape-shifter in the set is uno.

Buying is where M1's plural finally earns its keep: café → cafés, libro → libros, manzana → manzanas. Add -s to a vowel, -es to a consonant, and the article goes plural with it — los cafés, las manzanas.

sentences.cue: How much does the coffee cost?

words.note: "How much", accented because it is asking — like qué, cómo and dónde. In front of cuesta it never changes. In front of a noun it agrees with that noun: cuántos libros, cuántas manzanas.

"It costs" — the verb belongs to the thing being sold, not to you, so it is cuesta for one thing and cuestan for several. The answer names a number and the local money, and that word changes from country to country (euro, peso, sol, quetzal), so this course does not pick one for you.

sentences.trap: English asks "how much DOES IT cost" and puts a doing-word in front of the buyer. Spanish asks how much the coffee costs — the coffee is doing the costing, and there is no word for "does".
sentences.sound: CUÁN-to CUES-ta. The cu is a kw, and both words keep their stress on the first syllable.

variations.cue: How much does the apple cost?
variations.changed: a feminine noun — cuesta does not care

variations.cue: How much does the book cost?
variations.changed: swap what you are pricing

mistake.why: cuesto would be "I cost". The coffee is what costs: cuesta.

sentences.usage: The first thing you say at any counter.
sentences.mnemonic: The thing does the costing, so the thing picks the ending.

sentences.cue: How much do the books cost?

words.note: The plural of cuesta, and the -n is there because the BOOKS are plural. Exactly the shape of M1's me gusta → me gustan: the thing decides, every time.

sentences.trap: cuánto does not go plural with the books — only the verb does. ¿Cuántos libros hay? is a different question, about how many there are.
sentences.sound: CUES-tan. Adding the syllable does not move the stress: it stays where cuesta had it.

variations.cue: How much do the apples cost?
variations.changed: feminine plural — the verb is unchanged

variations.cue: How much do two coffees cost?
variations.changed: price a quantity rather than the shelf

mistake.why: cuánto only agrees when it sits in front of a noun. Here it is "how much" and stays put: ¿Cuánto cuestan los libros?

sentences.usage: Pricing more than one of something.
sentences.mnemonic: gustan, cuestan — the -n belongs to the things.

words.note: Two. Numbers from dos upwards never change shape for gender: dos cafés, dos manzanas.
Two words, one politeness — literally "for a favour". It travels whole and lives at the edge of the request, most often at the end after a comma. Neither half is worth learning on its own.

sentences.trap: Quiero is not rude in Spanish the way a flat "I want" is in English, and por favor is what keeps it courteous. Add the comma in writing — it is what marks the politeness off from the order.
sentences.sound: por fa-VOR. Both r's are single taps, and the stress lands on the last syllable of favor.

variations.cue: I'd like one coffee, please
variations.changed: one, so un in front of the noun

variations.cue: Please, I'd like two coffees
variations.changed: the other edge — it works at the front too

mistake.why: Two of them is a plural: dos cafés.

sentences.mnemonic: por favor rides at the edge, never in the middle.

sentences.cue: I'd like a kilo of apples

words.note: A kilo. Masculine — un kilo — and one of the very few Spanish words with a k in it, because it was borrowed. What you are buying comes after de, with no article: un kilo de manzanas.

sentences.trap: No article after de. un kilo de manzanas, not *un kilo de las manzanas — that would be a kilo of those particular apples on that shelf.
sentences.sound: KI-lo. The k is a plain k, and the single l is light — nothing like the English "kill".

variations.cue: I'd like two kilos of apples
variations.changed: the measure goes plural, de stays

variations.cue: I'd like a kilo of bread
variations.changed: swap what is being weighed

mistake.why: The de is what joins the measure to the goods: un kilo de manzanas.

sentences.mnemonic: measure + de + goods. The de never goes missing.

sentences.display: Una botella de agua, por favor

words.note: Bottle. Feminine: una botella. The ll is a y sound across nearly all of the Spanish-speaking world, and a sh in and around Buenos Aires.

sentences.trap: A whole request with no verb in it. Naming what you want plus por favor is complete and polite — Spanish does not need "can I have" in front of it.
sentences.sound: bo-TE-lla, stressed in the middle. The b at the start is a firm b; between vowels it would soften.

variations.cue: I'd like a bottle of water
variations.changed: the same request with the verb back in

variations.display: Dos botellas de agua, por favor
variations.cue: Two bottles of water, please
variations.changed: the measure goes plural

mistake.why: de joins the container to what is in it: una botella de agua.

sentences.usage: The order you will place most often in a hot country.
sentences.mnemonic: botella de agua — bottle OF water, always the of.

words.note: The number standing on its own, with nothing after it. Put a noun behind it and it must shorten: un libro (m), una mesa (f). This is the same word as M3's un — uno is simply its full shape.

sentences.trap: Pointing at something and saying "one" is uno. The moment you name the thing, uno cannot survive: *Quiero uno libro is wrong — it is Quiero un libro.
sentences.sound: U-no, two clean syllables. The Spanish u is always the oo of "food", never the English "yoo".

variations.cue: I'd like two, please
variations.changed: dos needs no shortening — only uno does

variations.cue: I'd like a coffee, please
variations.changed: name the thing and uno becomes un

mistake.why: In front of a noun it is un: Quiero un café.

sentences.mnemonic: uno alone, un before a noun.

sentences.display: Hay diez libros en la tienda
sentences.cue: There are ten books in the shop
sentences.glossEn: lit. "There-is ten books in the shop"
sentences.literal: There-is ten books in the shop

words.note: Ten. The counting road from here is dos, tres, cuatro, cinco, seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez, then veinte and cien — vocabulary rather than grammar, since none of them changes shape.

sentences.trap: M7's hay still does not go plural, even in front of ten books. Hay libros, hay diez libros, hay cien libros — one shape for all of them.
sentences.sound: One syllable, DIEZ, with the ie run together. The final z is an s across Latin America and a th in most of Spain.

variations.display: Hay dos libros en la mesa
variations.cue: There are two books on the table
variations.changed: swap the number and the place

variations.cue: Are there books in the shop?
variations.changed: the question, with no number at all

mistake.display: Hayn diez libros en la tienda
mistake.why: hay has no plural. It is hay whatever follows it.

sentences.mnemonic: hay never counts — the number does that.

words.note: Eight — the number on its own. You have already met it inside M4's las ocho, where it was the hour; here it is a quantity, and it looks the same because numbers never change shape.

sentences.trap: las ocho is eight o'clock and ocho manzanas is eight apples. The number is identical; the las in front of it is what makes it a time.
sentences.sound: O-cho. The ch is the ch of English "church", and the o's are short and pure.

variations.cue: I'd like eight, please
variations.changed: drop the noun — numbers other than uno need no change

variations.cue: I eat at eight
variations.changed: the same eight, back in its clock phrase from M4

mistake.why: A number above one takes a plural noun: ocho manzanas.

sentences.mnemonic: las ocho tells time; ocho counts things.

words.note: "Very", and it only ever stands in front of an adjective: muy caro, muy fría, muy ocupado. It never changes shape and it never attaches to a verb — that job belongs to M1's mucho (trabajo mucho).
Expensive, and it agrees with the thing priced: el libro es caro, la manzana es cara, los libros son caros. The opposite is barato.

sentences.trap: es caro and está caro are both correct and mean different things: es caro is an expensive thing, está caro is dear at the moment. The general statement — the one you make about a shelf — is es.
sentences.sound: CA-ro, with ONE tap of the r. Two taps makes carro, a different word altogether — the car, in much of Latin America.

variations.cue: The apple is very expensive
variations.changed: feminine noun, so cara — muy does not move

variations.cue: The books are very expensive
variations.changed: plural all the way through, and es becomes son

mistake.why: In front of an adjective it is muy: El libro es muy caro.

sentences.usage: The half of shopping that is not buying.
sentences.mnemonic: muy before an adjective, mucho with a noun or a verb.

words.note: "Everything", standing alone as one lump — which is why the verb stays singular: cuesta, not cuestan. In front of a noun it agrees with it instead: todo el día (M6), toda la casa.

sentences.trap: Everything is a lot of things and still counts as one: ¿Cuánto cuesta todo? A learner reaching for cuestan is agreeing with the shopping bag rather than with the word in the sentence.
sentences.sound: TO-do. The d between two vowels is soft, close to the th of English "the".

variations.cue: How much does everything cost, please?
variations.changed: the polite edge, inside the question marks

variations.cue: Everything is very expensive
variations.changed: the same todo as the subject of a statement

mistake.why: todo is one word standing for one lump: ¿Cuánto cuesta todo?

sentences.usage: The last question at the counter.
sentences.mnemonic: todo is singular, however much is in the bag.
